subsystems.name: Servicer spacecraft
subsystems.role: a free-flying robot that carries the arms, tools and fuel to a client satellite and holds position beside it.

subsystems.name: Robotic manipulators
subsystems.role: arms that grasp, hold and move hardware while bolted joints are undone and connections remade.

subsystems.name: Grapple and docking interfaces
subsystems.role: the mechanical, electrical and fluid couplings that let two spacecraft join and transfer propellant or power.

subsystems.name: Orbital replacement units and tooling
subsystems.role: hardware designed to be swapped by a robot rather than built to last forever.

subsystems.name: Relative navigation and autonomy software
subsystems.role: works out exactly where the client is and how to approach it without collision, with or without ground control.

subsystems.name: Ground test and mission infrastructure
subsystems.role: lets engineers rehearse the whole operation before launch.

buildSteps.title: Fix the interfaces first
buildSteps.detail: Before any robot is built, agree a standard grapple fixture, docking ring, refuelling port and data connector so future servicers can work on satellites from different makers. This standardisation is the real engineering bottleneck.

buildSteps.title: Design the servicer
buildSteps.detail: Size a spacecraft that can reach the target orbit, carry enough propellant for both itself and the client, and hold station within centimetres for hours.

buildSteps.title: Build the arms and tools
buildSteps.detail: Arms are assembled from lightweight composite and metal segments with geared joints, then fitted with grippers, cutting tools and fluid couplers matched to the client's hardware.

buildSteps.title: Rehearse on the ground
buildSteps.detail: Operators practise the full sequence in a neutral-buoyancy pool and on air-bearing tables, while the spacecraft is shaken, heated and frozen in vacuum chambers to prove it survives launch and orbit.

buildSteps.title: Launch and check out
buildSteps.detail: The servicer rides to orbit inside a fairing, deploys its solar arrays and antennas, and runs weeks of self-tests before any approach.

buildSteps.title: Rendezvous and inspect
buildSteps.detail: The servicer drifts up to the client over several days, using cameras and LIDAR to build a 3D model and confirm nothing is tumbling or damaged.

buildSteps.title: Capture and connect
buildSteps.detail: The arm or docking ring grabs the grapple fixture, dampens any residual motion, and pulls the two spacecraft into a rigid, electrically and fluidically connected stack.

buildSteps.title: Carry out the service
buildSteps.detail: Refuelling transfers propellant through the quick-disconnects; alternatively the robot unbolts a spent battery or instrument and installs a replacement from its cargo.

buildSteps.title: For assembly, repeat
buildSteps.detail: Larger structures are built by launching segments that each fit an existing fairing, then berthing them to a growing truss or backbone, one robot-joined node at a time.

prerequisites.why: proven between crewed and cargo vehicles and by commercial life-extension spacecraft; without it a servicer cannot reach its client.
refuelling and berthing interfaces exist in demonstrations but are not yet common on commercial satellites, so most targets cannot be serviced.
space station arms have built and repaired hardware for decades; transferable to free-flying servicers.
needed to approach an uncooperative or unknown target safely; demonstrated in inspection missions but not routine.
today's satellites are usually sealed at launch, so the benefit of servicing cannot be captured without redesigning them.

pathway.milestone: commercial life-extension spacecraft dock with working satellites and take over their station-keeping
pathway.unlocks: a market for servicing, and confidence that docking two commercial spacecraft works.

pathway.milestone: robotic refuelling and inspection of derelict or uncooperative objects in orbit
pathway.unlocks: the ability to work on satellites that were never designed to be visited.

pathway.milestone: robotic assembly of large antennas and observatories from modular parts
pathway.unlocks: spacecraft larger than any rocket fairing, which is the binding limit today.

pathway.milestone: routine in-orbit assembly, repair and recycling at scale
pathway.unlocks: infrastructure such as large solar arrays, habitable modules and telescopes built up over multiple launches.
